title: The Ledger of Windrow House
premise: Mara Amberdale has spent seven years as the night dispatcher for Windrow Taxi, listening to the town's confessions disguised as pickup requests and filing them away in her meticulous ledgers. When a drowned man is found on the riverbank wearing clothes stolen from her own closet, she realizes someone is using her invisibility as a weapon—and that the victim's death mirrors a drowning thirty years earlier at Windrow House. Following threads through old dispatch logs, anniversary dinner guest lists, and a retired constable's suppressed report, Mara uncovers a cover-up protected by the town's most respected families. In the end, she chooses justice outside the law: rather than hand the killer to police who buried the original crime, she exposes everything publicly at the thirtieth-anniversary dinner, sacrificing her own safety and a fragile love with Detective Ivo Renner to force the truth into daylight.
about_author: Freya Dunmore is the pen name of a former small-town court stenographer who spent a decade transcribing other people's worst nights before turning them into fiction. She writes mysteries about quiet people who keep records, and lives in a coastal village where everyone knows everyone's business except their own.

chapters.title: The Night Book
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. A routine shift establishes Windrow's rhythms: drunk calls, midnight pickups, Mara's ledger of secrets. Her last fare of the night is a nervous man asking to be taken to Windrow House and never arriving. Emotional beat: quiet competence masking loneliness; the reader senses her habit of watching without being seen.

chapters.title: Clothes That Weren't Hers
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Police wake her: a body on the riverbank wearing her cardigan, her scarf, her boots—clothes stolen from her closet while she worked. Detective Ivo Renner, an old flame, takes her statement. Emotional beat: violation and vertigo; the invisible woman made visible in the worst way.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Fridays
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. She searches her own flat for what else was touched and finds a page torn from one of her older ledgers—the year 1995. Flashback fragments surface: a summer drowning at Windrow House ruled accidental. Emotional beat: dread blooming into purpose.

chapters.title: The Anniversary Guest List
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. The victim is identified as Edmund Voss, son of the family that owns Windrow House, back in town for the estate's thirtieth-anniversary dinner. Every suspect was a child there the summer of the first drowning. Emotional beat: the past pressing its shape against the present.

chapters.title: Fares and Confessions
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. She re-reads seven years of dispatch logs, finding that half the town has confessed something to a taxi dispatcher at 3 a.m. Three separate passengers mentioned Windrow House. Emotional beat: the ledger transforms from coping mechanism to weapon.

chapters.title: Ivo's Cold File
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Ivo Renner. Ivo pulls the 1995 file and finds the investigating constable's notes were doctored; his own mentor signed off on the ruling. He hides this from Mara to protect her. Emotional beat: duty beginning to war with conscience—and with love.

chapters.title: The Gardener Remembers
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. She interviews Halcyon Brandt, the estate's ancient gardener, who recalls two children by the pond that night, not one. He names a girl who 'went away to school' afterward and never returned. Emotional beat: grief for a childhood destroyed by adult cowardice.

chapters.title: A Farewell in the Rain
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Someone follows Mara home from the archive; a warning note quotes her own ledger entries back at her. She realizes the killer has access to her cab company's records—or wrote them. Emotional beat: fear sharpening into defiance.

chapters.title: The Second Ledger
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. She discovers her predecessor, dispatcher Ruth Calloway, kept a parallel private log of suspicious fares until her disappearance in 2016. Ruth's last entry: 'Windrow pays for silence. Ask the daughter.' Emotional beat: kinship with a vanished woman who asked the same questions.

chapters.title: Dinner at Eight
chapters.summary: Mara's POV under pretext of a catering delivery. The Voss anniversary rehearsal: matriarch Odile Voss presiding, heirs circling, a portrait of the drowned boy from 1995 turned discreetly to the wall. Emotional beat: opulence as camouflage; Mara cataloguing lies like fares.

chapters.title: What the Daughter Knew
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. She locates Ruth Calloway alive, hiding in a neighboring county. Ruth reveals she witnessed the 1995 cover-up as a young woman and fled when Odile bought her silence. Emotional beat: terror and relief entwined; the cost of staying silent for thirty years.

chapters.title: Alibi, Woven
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Ivo maps alibis for the night Edmund died and finds they interlock too perfectly—every heir vouching for another, a lattice built in advance. He suspects the family knew Edmund intended to confess. Emotional beat: professional certainty colliding with loyalty to the force.

chapters.title: The Pond in Winter
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Mara visits the drained pond and finds a child's shoe corroded in the silt—physical proof the 1995 drowning involved struggle. Photographing it, she is nearly caught by the estate's security chief. Emotional beat: evidence as both shield and target.

chapters.title: Two Names in One Closet
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Forensics confirms the clothes worn by Edmund were altered to fit him—staged by someone with intimate knowledge of her wardrobe and shifts. The list narrows to current employees of the cab company. Emotional beat: betrayal inside the one place she felt safe.

chapters.title: The Dispatcher Before Ruth
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Digging into company history, Mara learns the night dispatcher in 1995 was Odile Voss's sister, who quietly funneled information to the family for decades. The rot predates everyone Mara trusted. Emotional beat: disillusionment deepening; institutions as accomplices.

chapters.title: Confession at 3 A.M.
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. A panicked late-night caller asks to be picked up near Windrow House, then hangs up. Tracing the call, Mara identifies the security chief, Dane Mercer—who was the second child at the pond in 1995 and has been killing to bury it. Emotional beat: the trap closing from both directions.

chapters.title: Taken
chapters.summary: Mercer's POV (brief, chilling). Mercer abducts Mara, intending her death to mirror Edmund's—another frame job using her own belongings. He explains, almost tenderly, that he killed to protect Odile, whom he loved. Emotional beat: horror refracted through warped devotion.

chapters.title: The River Knows
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Bound in the boathouse, Mara stalls Mercer by reciting his own 3 a.m. confessions from memory, cracking his certainty. Ivo, having finally defied his mentor and followed the ledger trail, arrives; Mercer flees into the marsh. Emotional beat: words as survival; love arriving late but arriving.

chapters.title: What Justice Costs
chapters.summary: Mara and Ivo's alternating POV. Ivo can arrest Mercer quietly and let the 1995 ruling stand; Mara refuses—Odile and the complicit constable must fall too. They quarrel bitterly over law versus truth. Emotional beat: love against duty at its sharpest; both right, both wounded.

chapters.title: The Anniversary Dinner
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. At the gala, before two hundred guests, Mara stands and reads aloud from thirty years of ledgers: the drowning, the payments, the doctored report, Edmund's murder. Odile rises to deny it and is met by Ruth Calloway walking in on Ivo's arm. Emotional beat: catharsis; the invisible woman making a whole town see.

chapters.title: After the Toast
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs briefly. Mercer surrenders at the pond where it began; Odile is arrested mid-toast; the constable's family returns his disgraced medal to the station. Mara testifies, exhausted and unhidden. Emotional beat: justice achieved outside the law's tidy channels, at real price.

chapters.title: The Last Entry
chapters.summary: Mara's POV. Weeks later, Mara closes her final ledger and starts a blank book—not of others' secrets now, but her own life. Ivo waits with coffee and no agenda. The pond is fenced, the house sold, the town raw but honest. Emotional beat: quiet hope; visibility chosen, not imposed.
